howto.name: How to reduce UDAP exposure for an AI product

steps.name: List every claim the product makes about itself
steps.text: Collect capability claims from marketing, sales decks, RFP responses, documentation and investor materials. These are all representations, not just the website.

steps.name: Substantiate each claim or change it
steps.text: For each claim, identify the evidence that it is true as stated. A claim you cannot evidence today is the one to rewrite, not defend.

steps.name: Review persona and credential signals
steps.text: Check what the system says about itself, what its name and avatar imply, and how it responds when asked whether it is a professional. Implied credentials are the trigger.

steps.name: Disclose synthetic media
steps.text: Anywhere a generated voice, face, person or testimonial reaches a consumer, disclose it. Absence of intent to deceive is not a defence to non-disclosure.

steps.name: Design against foreseeable misuse
steps.text: Write down how the product could predictably be misused, especially by vulnerable users and minors, and what safeguards exist for each. The written record is the point.

steps.name: Re-test after every model change
steps.text: A model swap can change persona behaviour and capability without any change to the marketing. Re-run the claim and persona checks whenever the underlying model changes.

short: Every state has an unfair-or-deceptive-practices statute that already reaches AI. Attorneys general are using them against overstated capability claims, chatbots posing as licensed professionals, undisclosed synthetic media, and foreseeable harm to users. No new law is required and none is being waited for.
title: State AG Enforcement Under UDAP
subtitle: Unfair or Deceptive Acts and Practices applied to AI, without new legislation
body_html:
The most active AI enforcement in the United States is being done under laws that never mention AI. Every state has an Unfair or Deceptive Acts and Practices statute — a UDAP law — and attorneys general are applying it to AI systems the way they would to any other commercial product. If a tool misleads a consumer, overstates what it can do, or causes foreseeable harm, that is already actionable. No new legislation is required, and no state is waiting for one.

This matters more than the statute-watching most compliance programmes do. A company can be fully compliant with Colorado SB 26-189, Texas HB 149 and the Utah disclosure duty and still be exposed on day one, because UDAP reaches conduct those statutes never address and applies in all fifty states at once.

Four theories, and what triggers each

1. Overstated capability, or "AI washing"

The claim is the product. Saying a system is fully automated when people are doing the work behind it, describing an algorithm as free of bias without evidence, or advertising accuracy the system does not achieve are ordinary deception claims that happen to involve AI. The exposure is not confined to marketing copy: capability claims in sales decks, RFP responses, investor materials and API documentation are all representations to somebody.

The practical test is simple and uncomfortable. For each claim your product makes about itself, could you produce evidence to a regulator today? Not evidence that it works, evidence that it works as described. Substantiation is the standard, and it is the same standard applied to a supplement label.

2. Substituting for a licensed professional

This is the theory moving fastest. Using AI as an assistive tool is unremarkable; presenting a chatbot as a substitute for a lawyer, doctor, therapist or financial adviser is a different act, and it triggers both UDAP and the state's licensing regime at once. Attorneys general have sought injunctive relief against AI products whose chatbots presented themselves as licensed clinicians and offered treatment recommendations.

The line is drawn by what the system says about itself and how the product is marketed, not by what it technically does. A model that gives careful, hedged information while stating plainly that it is not a clinician sits on one side. The same model given a title, a credential, or a persona that implies one sits on the other. Persona design is a legal decision.

3. Undisclosed synthetic media

Deepfakes, cloned voices and generated testimonials are deceptive when the audience is not told. This covers outright scams, and it also covers commercial uses that feel harmless: an AI customer service agent presented as a named person, a product testimonial from someone who does not exist, a generated endorsement in a voice the audience recognises. Failure to disclose is the violation; malicious intent is not required.

4. Foreseeable misuse and product safety

The newest and broadest theory. UDAP has long carried an expectation that a company build reasonable safeguards against foreseeable misuse of its product, and that expectation is now being applied to AI. A bipartisan coalition of more than forty state attorneys general has pressed AI developers to strengthen protections in companion chatbots, particularly where minors are users, against outputs that encourage self-harm or reinforce delusion. Individual attorneys general have opened investigations into whether a developer bears responsibility for a chatbot's role in real-world harm.

What makes this theory demanding is that it is not about accuracy at all. A system can be truthful, well-documented and correctly disclosed, and still fail here if a foreseeable pattern of misuse was not designed against.

Why this is harder to plan for than a statute

A statute tells you its scope, its effective date and its penalty. UDAP tells you none of those. It applies in every state, it applies now, its scope is whatever a court will accept as unfair or deceptive, and the enforcer is an elected official with discretion about which matters to bring. Fifty attorneys general can reach different conclusions about the same product.

The compliance response is therefore not a checklist against a text. It is a habit: every claim substantiated, every persona reviewed for implied credentials, every synthetic output disclosed, and every foreseeable misuse designed against and documented. Those four habits answer all fifty statutes at once, and they are also what the FTC applies federally under Section 5 — see FTC AI enforcement.

How the states act together, and why that changes the exposure

State attorneys general rarely investigate a major AI company alone. They form multistate coalitions, and the practical consequence is that a company facing state enforcement is usually facing dozens of states at once, through one lead office, on one document demand. Planning against the statute of a single state while ignoring the coalition mechanism understates the exposure badly.

NAAG is the coordinating layer

The National Association of Attorneys General provides the standing structure: working groups, shared intelligence, and a multistate task force that coordinates litigation across offices. It is where a pattern noticed in one state becomes an investigation joined by forty. There is no equivalent on the defence side. The states are organised; the targets are not.

Lead states do the work, signatories supply the weight

A coalition designates one or a few lead states to head an executive committee. Those offices commit the staff attorneys and technical experts and run the day-to-day investigation, while the remaining states sign on, contributing jurisdiction rather than labour. Fifty offices never duplicate one investigation, which is exactly why the model scales.

The clearest example to date: on 12 June 2026, New York Attorney General Letitia James served OpenAI with a subpoena on behalf of a bipartisan coalition of 42 state attorneys general, the broadest coordinated state action yet brought against an AI company. The demand reached advertising practices, user engagement and retention design, consumer and health data handling, treatment of minors and seniors, internal policies, and the behaviour of the models themselves, including sycophancy. The coalition also wrote to Meta, Anthropic, Google and xAI warning that developers may be held accountable for what their generative products produce.

Two features of that demand are worth dwelling on. It arrived days after a confidential IPO filing, which is when a documentary demand is most expensive to receive. And it named a model behaviour, sycophancy, as a subject of consumer-protection inquiry. That moves regulatory attention from what a company claims to how the system is built and tuned.

Coordinated discovery

Coalitions issue joint civil investigative demands or subpoenas. A demand from one state can be contested on jurisdiction or scope; a demand carrying dozens of signatures is far harder to resist, and the cost of analysing complex technical production is split across offices that also pool subject-matter expertise. The asymmetry favours the states, and it is structural rather than incidental.

One bloc at settlement

The coalition negotiates as a unit. For the states this multiplies leverage, since the threat is simultaneous penalty exposure across most of the national market. For the company it offers the one thing worth having: a global resolution rather than dozens of separate fights. That trade is why multistate matters so often end in a single settlement carrying substantial restitution and binding conduct commitments that then apply nationwide.

The binding-conduct half is the part to plan around. Financial terms are finite and survivable. Injunctive terms reshape the product, and they usually last years.

Where specific matters are tracked

Named enforcement actions and private suits, with docket numbers and status, are in the AI lawsuit tracker. Statutes with named regulators are covered under state AI laws, and the enforcers themselves under agency enforcement.
seo_title: State AG UDAP Enforcement Against AI: The Law That Already Applies
meta_description: Every state has a UDAP statute, and attorneys general are applying them to AI now. Four enforcement theories, what triggers each, and why waiting for an AI law is the wrong plan.
